steps.explanationAfterStep: Three π bonds become two new σ bonds and one new π bond in a single step, through a six-membered cyclic transition state. No intermediate and no charges: the arrows could just as well be drawn round the ring the other way. Swapping two π bonds for two σ bonds is what makes the reaction downhill.

title: Diels–Alder reaction of butadiene and ethene
subtitle: Six electrons move round a ring in one step
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 34

reactants.caption: buta-1,3-diene (drawn s-cis) + ethene
hintTiers: Count the π electrons: two π bonds in the diene and one in ethene, six electrons that can move round a ring of six atoms. Which carbons of the diene can reach ethene?
Three arrows, all in one step. The two end carbons of the diene each make a new σ bond to an ethene carbon, and a new C=C appears between the diene's two middle carbons.

Arrow 1: from one diene π bond to a new bond between its end carbon and an ethene carbon. Arrow 2: from the other diene π bond to the bond between the two middle carbons. Arrow 3: from the ethene π bond to a new bond between the other ethene carbon and the other end of the diene.
reactants.learnerPrompt: The diene and ethene join in a single step to make a six-membered ring. Draw every arrow of that one step.

misconceptions.arrowPattern: π C1-C2 -> σ C1-C6; π C5-C6 -> σ C2-C5
misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That makes a four-membered ring from one diene π bond and ethene: a [2+2] cycloaddition. Two alkenes do not do this on heating (it needs light). Use both π bonds of the diene so that six atoms form the ring.
Only the two end carbons of the diene make new bonds. The middle two carbons end up joined by the new C=C double bond.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right start: one end of the diene bonds to ethene. The middle carbon has now lost its π bond, so in the same step the other π bonds move as well. Two more arrows.

conditionsLabel: heat · pressure (slow: ethene has no activating group)
mechanismSummary: The Diels–Alder reaction is a [4+2] cycloaddition: four π electrons of the diene and two of the dienophile move together round a six-membered ring, making two σ bonds and a new π bond between the diene's middle carbons. The diene must be able to take the s-cis conformation so its ends can reach the dienophile. Ethene is a poor dienophile (no electron-withdrawing group lowers its LUMO), so this parent reaction needs heat and pressure and gives low yields; the next reactions use better partners.
